cards.heading: A ParkingSpot hierarchy, not a type field
cards.hook: Handicapped, Compact, Large, and MotorcycleSpot each extend an abstract ParkingSpot with its own assignVehicle — not one class branching on a spot-type enum.

cards.heading: Vehicle hierarchy mirrors the spot hierarchy
cards.hook: Car, Van, Truck, and Motorcycle each extend Vehicle with their own assignTicket — polymorphism decides which spot type a vehicle can use, not a chain of if-checks.

cards.heading: Singleton for the one parking lot
cards.hook: ParkingLot.getInstance() guarantees a single shared lot instance across entrances, exits, and display boards — there's only ever one physical lot to coordinate.

cards.heading: A ticket's lifecycle is its own enum
cards.hook: ISSUED, IN_USE, PAID, VALIDATED, CANCELED, REFUNDED — modeling ticket status as a closed set of states makes an invalid transition a type error, not a runtime surprise.

cards.heading: Composition: a ticket owns its payment
cards.hook: ParkingTicket holds a Payment instance directly — the ticket's lifetime and its payment record are tied together, unlike the looser vehicle-to-spot association.

cards.heading: Payment methods as a polymorphic hierarchy
cards.hook: Cash and CreditCard both extend an abstract Payment with initiateTransaction() — adding a third payment method means one new subclass, not a new branch in existing code.

cards.heading: Pricing lives in its own class
cards.hook: ParkingRate.calculate(duration, vehicle, spot) is a separate object from ParkingLot, not a method bolted onto it — rate logic can change independently of how the lot itself is modeled.

cards.heading: Entrance and Exit are their own classes
cards.hook: getTicket() and validateTicket() live on dedicated Entrance/Exit classes rather than ParkingLot — multiple physical entry/exit points can each hold their own id without bloating the lot object.

cards.heading: Capacity is a hard constraint, not a suggestion
cards.hook: A 40,000-vehicle lot has to reject entry outright once full, and show that state at every entrance and board — the system has to know it's full before a vehicle shows up, not after.

cards.heading: Design for configurable, tiered pricing up front
cards.hook: First hour at one rate, the next two at another, every hour after that cheaper still — a pricing model needs to support tiered rates per vehicle and spot type from day one, not bolted on later.

cards.heading: DisplayBoard aggregates spot availability
cards.hook: A DisplayBoard holds a map of spot type to available spots and recomputes on update — the board doesn't own spots, it just reflects the lot's current state.

cards.heading: Admin as a privileged Account subtype
cards.hook: Admin extends Account and adds addParkingSpot/addEntrance/addExit — administrative capability is a distinct class, not a permission flag checked at runtime.

cards.heading: Multiple entrances and exits need independent tracking
cards.hook: A customer could pay on one floor and exit through a different panel entirely — payment state has to live on the ticket itself, not be assumed from a single linear entry-to-exit flow.

cards.heading: Abstract methods throw, not return undefined silently
cards.hook: ParkingSpot.assignVehicle() is marked abstract and must be overridden by each spot subtype — a forgotten override fails loudly instead of silently doing nothing.

cards.heading: A ticket references both its entrance and its exit
cards.hook: ParkingTicket stores both the Entrance and Exit instance a vehicle moved through — a later dispute about which gate was used never requires cross-referencing separate logs by timestamp.

cards.heading: Business logic lives in services, not models
cards.hook: Post, Story, and Comment stay thin data holders — PostService, StoryService, and CommentService own the actual business logic, keeping persistence and side effects out of the model classes.

cards.heading: Repositories isolate storage from everything else
cards.hook: PostRepository.save/findById/delete is the only thing that knows about the database — swap MySQL for DynamoDB and nothing above the repository layer has to change.

cards.heading: A feed score is a weighted sum, not just recency
cards.hook: Recency, engagement, poster relationship, and content quality are each weighted and summed into one score per post — recency alone would just surface whoever posts most often.

cards.heading: Recency decays exponentially, not linearly
cards.hook: A post's recency score uses exponential decay so very recent posts score sharply higher — a straight-line decay would treat a 2-hour-old post almost the same as a 20-hour-old one.

cards.heading: Engagement scores use log, not raw counts
cards.hook: log(1 + likes) keeps a post with 10,000 likes from completely drowning out one with 500 — diminishing returns on raw engagement stops the feed from being a pure popularity contest.

cards.heading: Feeds are cached per user, per page
cards.hook: feed:{userId}:{page} as a cache key with a 5-minute TTL means a user refreshing their feed repeatedly doesn't recompute the ranking algorithm every single time.

cards.heading: Factory pattern for post media types
cards.hook: MediaFactory.createMedia(type, file) returns a Photo or a Video based on type — the caller never has to know which concrete class it's getting back.

cards.heading: Observer pattern for notifications
cards.hook: NotificationService.subscribe(observer) lets likes, comments, and follows all fan out through the same notify() call — a new notification channel means adding an observer, not touching every action that triggers one.

cards.heading: Strategy pattern lets feed ranking be swappable
cards.hook: FeedRankingStrategy is an interface EngagementBasedRanking implements — A/B testing a different ranking algorithm means writing one new strategy class, not forking the whole feed service.

cards.heading: Stories expire by design, not by a cleanup job alone
cards.hook: Story.isExpired() checks its own expiresAt, set at creation time — the object itself knows when it's stale, and a background scheduler just acts on what the object already reports.

cards.heading: Nested comments via self-reference, not a tree structure
cards.hook: Comment.parentCommentId points back to another comment in the same table — a reply is just a comment with a parent, no separate tree data structure needed.

cards.heading: Likes are their own entity, not just a counter
cards.hook: A Like row stores who liked what and when, not just an incrementing count on the post — that's what makes 'did I already like this' and 'who liked this' both possible.

cards.heading: A unique constraint prevents double-liking
cards.hook: The likes table's unique key on (user_id, target_id, target_type) makes double-liking the same post impossible at the database level — no application-side check-then-insert race condition.

cards.heading: Private accounts gate visibility at the service layer
cards.hook: canUserViewPost checks whether the owner is private and, if so, whether the viewer actually follows them — visibility is computed per request, not a stored boolean on the post.

cards.heading: Following a private account creates a request, not a follow
cards.hook: followUser() branches on the target's isPrivate flag — a public account follow is immediate, a private one creates a pending follow request instead, same method, different outcome.

cards.heading: A typed error hierarchy carries its own status code
cards.hook: NotFoundError, UnauthorizedError, and ValidationError each extend a base error with a statusCode baked in — the middleware just reads err.statusCode, no giant if/else mapping error types to HTTP codes.

cards.heading: Hashtags get their own table and join table
cards.hook: Hashtags aren't parsed out of captions at read time — they're extracted once at write time into their own table plus a post_hashtags join table, so searching by hashtag is an indexed lookup, not a text scan.

cards.heading: Different data gets different cache lifetimes
cards.hook: Feeds cache for 5 minutes, profiles for 15, popular posts for an hour — the TTL matches how often each kind of data actually tends to change, not one blanket expiry for everything.

cards.heading: Comments and likes load lazily, not with the post
cards.hook: A post's comments and full likes list load on demand with their own pagination — fetching a feed of posts never means pulling every comment on every post along with it.

cards.heading: Deleting a post means deleting its media too
cards.hook: PostService.deletePost() deletes from media storage before deleting the database row — the two deletes are sequenced so you never end up with an orphaned file and no record pointing to it.

cards.heading: A service composes other services, not every repository directly
cards.hook: FeedService depends on FeedGenerator, which depends on the post/like/comment repositories — ranking logic is isolated in its own class instead of living inside the thing that serves the feed.

cards.heading: A Follow relationship can be blocked without being deleted
cards.hook: Follow.status toggles between active and blocked rather than deleting the row outright — the history of the relationship survives a block/unblock cycle.

cards.heading: Base62 encoding, not random strings
cards.hook: A short code is a counter value encoded in base62 (0-9a-zA-Z) — an auto-incrementing counter turned into 5-7 characters, instead of a random string that then needs a collision check.

cards.heading: A counter-based code never collides
cards.hook: Because each short code comes from a strictly increasing counter, two different long URLs can never land on the same code — hashing the URL instead would need a collision-retry loop that counter-based generation skips entirely.

cards.heading: Custom aliases and generated codes share one field
cards.hook: shortCode holds either a generated base62 value or a user's custom alias, with isCustom as the only differentiator — one code path handles redirect and lookup regardless of how the code was created.

cards.heading: Cache-aside: check cache, fall through to DB
cards.hook: getLongURL tries the cache first, and only on a miss hits the database and refills the cache — the cache is a read-through convenience, never the system of record.

cards.heading: Hot URLs get longer cache lifetimes
cards.hook: The top 20% most-clicked URLs get a 24-hour cache TTL instead of the default 1 hour — cache budget goes where traffic actually concentrates, following an 80/20 split.

cards.heading: Click tracking is fire-and-forget
cards.hook: redirect() returns the long URL immediately and tracks the click asynchronously in the background — a slow analytics write never adds latency to the one thing a user is actually waiting on.

cards.heading: Clicks flow through a message queue, not a direct write
cards.hook: A click event publishes to a queue rather than writing straight to the analytics table — a traffic spike queues up instead of overwhelming the database with synchronous writes.

cards.heading: Token bucket rate limiting, not a fixed counter
cards.hook: Tokens refill continuously at a fixed rate instead of a counter that resets all at once every hour — a token bucket smooths out bursts instead of allowing a thundering herd right at the reset boundary.
cards.code:
const tokensToAdd = elapsedSeconds * refillRate;
const newTokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + tokensToAdd);

cards.heading: Strategy pattern for redirect type
cards.hook: PermanentRedirectStrategy returns a 301, TemporaryRedirectStrategy a 302 — whether a short link redirects permanently or temporarily is a swappable strategy, not a hardcoded status code.

cards.heading: Factory pattern picks the short-code generator
cards.hook: ShortCodeGeneratorFactory.create('counter' | 'hash' | 'random', ...) returns the right generator implementation — the service that needs a short code doesn't know or care which algorithm produced it.

cards.heading: Every URL gets validated before it's shortened
cards.hook: URLValidator checks format, then checks a blacklist, then checks for malware and phishing — three independent checks before a URL is allowed to be shortened at all, not just a regex for 'is this a URL'.

cards.heading: Each failure mode gets its own typed error
cards.hook: URLNotFoundError (404), URLExpiredError (410), AliasExistsError (409), RateLimitExceededError (429) — the exact HTTP status is baked into the error class itself, so the catch-all handler never has to guess.

cards.heading: Analytics aggregate incrementally, not by replaying every click
cards.hook: Each new click event updates running totals (by date, country, referrer, device, browser) on an existing Analytics record — getting a summary never means scanning every historical click row.

cards.heading: Click events get partitioned by date
cards.hook: The click_events table is partitioned by year and month — a table logging every click on every short URL grows forever, and partitioning keeps queries scoped to recent partitions fast.

cards.heading: Observer pattern decouples click tracking from logging
cards.hook: AnalyticsObserver and LoggingObserver both subscribe to the same click event — adding something new that reacts to a click never means touching the code that fires the event.

cards.heading: A URL knows its own expiration
cards.hook: URL.isExpired() compares its own expiresAt to now — the service doesn't carry expiration logic separately, it just asks the object.

cards.heading: Only the creator can update or delete a URL
cards.hook: updateURL and deleteURL both check url.userId !== userId before doing anything — ownership is checked at the point of mutation, not assumed because the request carried an API key.

cards.heading: Deleting a URL is really deactivating it
cards.hook: deleteURL() calls url.deactivate() rather than removing the row — the short code and its click history stay intact for analytics even after a user 'deletes' their link.

cards.heading: Custom aliases get checked for collisions explicitly
cards.hook: A custom alias is checked against existing short codes before being accepted — generated codes never collide by construction, but a user-chosen alias absolutely can, so it needs its own existence check.

cards.heading: Premium accounts get a different limit, not a different system
cards.hook: upgradeToPremium() just raises rateLimit from 1,000 to 10,000 requests per hour — the same rate limiter and the same code path serve both tiers, only the number changes.

cards.heading: A separate counters table makes the sequence durable
cards.hook: The base62 encoder needs an ever-increasing number from somewhere durable — a dedicated counters table with atomic increments is that source of truth, not an in-memory variable that resets on restart.

cards.heading: Redirect and shortening are separate services
cards.hook: URLShortenerService creates and manages URLs; RedirectService only resolves and tracks clicks — a service that just needs to redirect never has to depend on alias-validation or expiration-update logic it doesn't use.

cards.heading: Instance state transitions are explicit, not implied
cards.hook: Each InstanceState lists exactly which states it can transition to — trying to start a RUNNING instance isn't just a bad idea the code happens to allow, canTransitionTo() makes it impossible.

cards.heading: An instance type's resource needs come from itself
cards.hook: InstanceType.getResourceRequirements() returns CPU, memory, network, and storage needs — placement logic asks the instance type what it needs rather than maintaining its own lookup table.

cards.heading: Instance families are derived, not stored
cards.hook: determineFamily() reads the first letter of the instance type name to classify it as general-purpose, compute-optimized, memory-optimized, and so on — the family is computed from the name, never a separately maintained field that could drift out of sync.

cards.heading: Volume IOPS and throughput are computed from type and size
cards.hook: calculateIOPS() derives performance characteristics from the volume type (gp3, io1, st1...) and size rather than storing them separately — gp3's formula alone is max(3000, size times 3), so a bigger disk earns more IOPS automatically.

cards.heading: Security group rules check protocol, port, and source together
cards.hook: evaluateIngress() only allows traffic if the protocol matches (or is wildcard), the port falls within the rule's range, and the source IP falls inside the rule's CIDR — all three conditions, not just one.

cards.heading: CIDR matching is bitwise, not string comparison
cards.hook: isIpInCidr masks both the rule's network and the incoming IP down to the same prefix length and compares the result — that's how '10.0.0.0/8 allows 10.5.3.2' gets decided without a library.
cards.code:
const mask = ~(2 ** (32 - prefixLength) - 1);
return (ipToNumber(network) & mask) === (ipToNumber(ip) & mask);

cards.heading: A hypervisor host tracks its own allocated vs total resources
cards.hook: HypervisorHost.canAllocate() checks allocated CPU/memory against totals before accepting a new instance — the host itself enforces it never gets oversubscribed, rather than trusting the scheduler to always get the math right.

cards.heading: Strategy pattern for instance placement
cards.hook: SpreadPlacementStrategy picks the host with the fewest instances, ClusterPlacementStrategy picks the one with the most — same interface, opposite goals, chosen per workload without touching the orchestration code around them.

cards.heading: Launching an instance returns before it's actually running
cards.hook: launchInstance() saves a PENDING instance and publishes an event, then returns immediately — placement, IP allocation, and host assignment all happen asynchronously, which is why a real instance takes time to go from pending to running.

cards.heading: Placement picks an AZ, then a host, then IPs — in that order
cards.hook: placeInstance() resolves availability zone first, preferring the subnet's own AZ, then asks the placement strategy for a host in that AZ, and only then allocates IPs — each step narrows the search before the next one runs.

cards.heading: Migrating an instance is deallocate-then-reallocate, not move
cards.hook: migrateInstance() finds a brand new host via placeInstance(), then deallocates resources from the old host — there's no 'move' operation, just a new placement followed by freeing the old reservation.

cards.heading: Billing reacts to lifecycle events, not a polling job
cards.hook: BillingService subscribes directly to InstanceRunning/Stopped/Terminated events — billing starts and stops exactly when the instance does, with no separate process polling instance states to catch changes.

cards.heading: Cost is hours times price, computed only at the end
cards.hook: calculateCost() multiplies elapsed hours by the per-hour rate once an instance stops — usage cost isn't tracked incrementally while running, it's derived once from a start and end timestamp.
cards.code:
const hours = (endTime - startTime) / (1000 * 60 * 60);
return hours * pricePerHour;

cards.heading: Retry with exponential backoff, but not for every error
cards.hook: retryWithBackoff() doubles its delay after each failure up to a cap, but explicitly skips retrying an InvalidStateTransitionException — retrying a request that's wrong by definition would never succeed no matter how many attempts.

cards.heading: Circuit breaker stops hammering a failing dependency
cards.hook: After 5 failures the circuit breaker flips OPEN and rejects calls instantly for 60 seconds, then allows one HALF_OPEN test request before fully closing again — a failing backend gets a recovery window instead of a continuous retry storm.

cards.heading: Resource tags as a Map, not fixed columns
cards.hook: Instance.tags is a Map of arbitrary key-value pairs, not a fixed set of columns — adding a new tag never requires a schema migration.

cards.heading: A security group rule needs a destination, always
cards.hook: validateRule() rejects a rule with neither a source CIDR nor a source security group — an ingress or egress rule that doesn't specify where traffic is allowed from or to isn't a rule, it's a mistake waiting to open everything.

cards.heading: Modifying instance type requires the instance to be stopped
cards.hook: modifyInstance() explicitly checks the instance is STOPPED before allowing instanceType to change — resizing a running instance isn't technically prevented anywhere else, so the check has to live right at the point of mutation.

cards.heading: A snapshot starts pending and fills in asynchronously
cards.hook: createSnapshot() writes a snapshot record with state 'pending' and progress 0, then kicks off the actual copy in the storage backend — the API returns fast, the snapshot catches up in the background.

cards.heading: Read replicas and caching both target the same hot path
cards.hook: Frequently-read instance and volume state goes through both a cache layer and read replicas — the two techniques solve the same read-heavy problem at different layers, cache first, replica behind it.

cards.heading: An Image (AMI) tracks its own lifecycle state too
cards.hook: Image has PENDING, AVAILABLE, DEREGISTERED, FAILED states just like Instance does — any long-lived resource in this system gets the same state-machine treatment, not just instances.

cards.heading: IP allocation is a dedicated service, not inline logic
cards.hook: allocatePrivateIp() and allocatePublicIp() are their own service calls during placement — IP address management is centralized in one place rather than scattered wherever an instance happens to need an address.

cards.heading: describeInstances filters client-side after one broad fetch
cards.hook: describeInstances() pulls all of an account's instances, then filters by instanceIds, states, and instanceTypes in memory — simple to read, though it assumes an account's instance count stays small enough that this never becomes the bottleneck.

cards.heading: Every domain error carries a real HTTP status code
cards.hook: Like the other case studies in this series, EC2's custom exceptions each hardcode their own status code at construction — the pattern repeats because it works: the error type is the single source of truth for how to respond.

cards.heading: Six design patterns, one system
cards.hook: State (instance lifecycle), Strategy (placement), Factory (instance creation), Observer (events), Repository (data access), and Singleton (shared services) all show up in the same design — each one solving a real problem that actually came up.

cards.heading: Utilization is the max of CPU and memory pressure, not the average
cards.hook: HypervisorHost.updateUtilization() takes the higher of CPU% and memory% utilization, not their average — a host maxed out on memory but idle on CPU is still a maxed-out host for placement purposes.

cards.heading: Instance IDs encode their own creation time
cards.hook: generateInstanceId() builds the id from Date.now() plus a random suffix — ids sort roughly chronologically for free, without needing a separate created-at index just to answer 'which instances are newest'.
